title: Using text evidence to draw conclusions
blurb: Draw the conclusion the text actually supports, then pick the one sentence that proves it most directly.
question: A TEAS passage says a clinic added Saturday hours and most Saturday visitors turned out to be existing patients. The question asks which sentence best supports the conclusion that the hours drew fewer new patients than expected. Two sentences mention Saturdays. How do you choose?

teach.body: Formally, a conclusion is a judgment reached by combining details in a text; it must be consistent with all of the relevant details and contradict none of them. Text evidence is the sentence or detail that most directly proves that judgment. In plain English: a conclusion is what the facts add up to, and the best evidence is the line you would point to if someone said, 'Prove it.'

(1) When Riverside Clinic began opening on Saturday mornings, managers expected the extra hours to attract new patients. (2) Instead, most Saturday visitors were existing patients who used to go to the emergency room for minor problems on weekends. (3) Clinic records show that weekend emergency room visits by its patients fell by nearly a third. (4) The extra shift cost more in staff wages than managers had planned. (5) Even so, the board voted in January to keep Saturday hours for another year.

root.label: Riverside passage
root.sub: Each conclusion has its own best proof

teach.caption: Every sentence is on topic. Only one is the best evidence for any given conclusion.

items: Restate the conclusion in a few words: 'Saturdays drew few new patients.'
For each option, ask: if this sentence were true, would it prove that exact claim?
Cross out sentences that are on topic but prove a different claim (sentence 4 proves cost, not who came).
Pick the sentence that proves the claim most directly, with the fewest extra steps (sentence 2).

teach.caption: Sentence 1 tells what managers expected; it says nothing about who actually came.

teach.h: A conclusion must fit every detail
teach.body: Test a conclusion against the whole passage, not one sentence. 'The board ended Saturday hours because they cost too much' fits sentence 4 but contradicts sentence 5, so it fails. 'Saturday hours were a failure' ignores sentence 3. The best-supported conclusion is the one that is most strongly backed by the text and clashes with nothing in it. Strong words such as 'proves', 'all' or 'every' need equally strong support.

bands.label: Must be true or strongly supported
Possible, but the text is silent

teach.caption: On the TEAS, 'could be true' is not enough. Choose the option the text backs most strongly.

teach.text: The classic trap is evidence that is on topic but supports a different claim. It shares key words with the conclusion, so it feels right. A second trap is a conclusion that uses absolute language ('all patients', 'proves') when the text only describes most patients or one clinic.

teach.h: Scenario: Jasmine works a two-part item
teach.body: Jasmine Okafor, applying to a BSN program, sees two linked items. Part 1 asks which conclusion is best supported. She rejects 'Saturday hours lost money for the clinic' because the passage says wages were higher than planned, not that the clinic lost money. She picks 'Saturday hours cut weekend emergency room visits by the clinic's patients.' Part 2 asks for the best evidence. Sentence 2 explains who came on Saturdays; sentence 3 measures the drop in emergency room visits. She chooses sentence 3, which proves that conclusion most directly.

steps.label: Part 1
steps.sub: Pick the conclusion that fits every detail

steps.label: Part 2
steps.sub: Find the sentence that proves that choice

steps.label: Cross-check
steps.sub: Does the evidence match Part 1 exactly?

items: A conclusion combines details and must contradict none of them.
The best evidence proves the exact claim, not just the topic.
On-topic sentences that prove a different claim are the main trap.
Prefer 'strongly supported' over 'possibly true'; distrust unearned absolutes.
In two-part items, the evidence you pick must prove the conclusion you picked.

summary: You can now draw a conclusion that fits every detail in a passage and choose the sentence that proves it most directly. You can also reject evidence that is merely on topic and conclusions that overreach the text.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Last fall, Grant High School moved its first bell from 7:30 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. By spring, first-period absences had dropped by about 20 percent, and the number of students marked late fell even more. Some coaches warned that practices would end too late in the evening, yet the number of students signing up for sports teams stayed about the same as the year before.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: The later bell improved attendance without lowering sports sign-ups.
The later bell raised student grades in most subjects by the spring.
Coaches persuaded the school to shorten its practices after the change.
Students slept about an hour longer each night after the later bell.
A.why: The passage reports fewer absences and fewer late students, and says sports sign-ups stayed about the same. The conclusion combines both details and goes no further.

whyNot.1: Grades are never mentioned; this conclusion has no support in the text.
whyNot.2: The coaches raised a concern, but nothing says practices were shortened.
whyNot.3: This may seem likely from outside knowledge, but the passage gives no sleep data.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) The Maplewood Public Library began lending free reading glasses at its front desk in March. (2) Staff had noticed patrons squinting at forms and newspapers. (3) By June, the desk had lent glasses more than 600 times. (4) Several patrons said they had been embarrassed to ask for help before. (5) The library buys the glasses in bulk for about two dollars a pair.

Which sentence best supports the conclusion that the program met a real need among patrons?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 5
Sentence 3
A.why: More than 600 loans in about three months shows patrons actually used the glasses, which is the most direct proof that the program met a real need.

whyNot.0: Sentence 1 only says when and where the program started; it shows nothing about demand.
whyNot.1: Sentence 2 explains why staff expected a need, but it does not show the need was met.
whyNot.2: Sentence 5 supports a conclusion about low cost, not about patron need.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Desmond took the bus to his nursing clinicals for the first month of the term. In October he began leaving home 40 minutes earlier, and his instructor noted that he had not been late once since. He told a classmate the earlier bus was less crowded, so he could review his notes on the ride.

Which conclusion is consistent with ALL of the details in the passage?
options: Desmond stopped taking the bus and began driving in October.
Desmond's change in routine helped both his timing and his study.
Desmond's instructor required him to arrive 40 minutes early.
Desmond was late to every clinical shift during the first month.
A.why: He has not been late since October, and the quieter bus lets him review notes. A conclusion covering both effects fits every detail.

whyNot.0: This contradicts the passage: he still takes a bus, just an earlier one.
whyNot.2: The instructor noted his punctuality; nothing says the instructor required the change.
whyNot.3: Overstatement: the passage implies he was sometimes late before, not late every time.

B.q:
Read the passage.

A hospital replaced the overhead paging system on two units with silent pagers that vibrate on each nurse's badge. On those units, nurses reported fewer interruptions during medication rounds. Patients' scores for 'quiet at night' rose from 61 to 78 percent over six months. On units that kept overhead paging, the same score barely changed.

Which sentence from the passage best supports the conclusion that the silent pagers, rather than some hospital-wide change, made the units quieter for patients?
options: Nurses on the two units reported fewer interruptions on rounds.
The hospital replaced paging with silent pagers on two units.
Units that kept overhead paging saw almost no change in scores.
The 'quiet at night' score on the two units rose to 78 percent.
B.why: The comparison with units that kept overhead paging rules out a hospital-wide cause: if everything had changed, those units would have improved too. That is the most direct support for the pagers being the reason.

whyNot.0: This concerns interruptions for nurses, a different claim from patient quiet.
whyNot.1: This describes the change but gives no result, so it proves nothing about cause.
whyNot.3: This shows the score rose but cannot rule out a hospital-wide cause on its own.

B.q:
Read the passage.

At Sunnyvale Elementary, the school nurse began sending home a one-page sheet on handwashing with every student who visited her office with a cold. Over the winter, her office logged 15 percent fewer visits for colds than the winter before. Parents of three students called to say the sheet was helpful.

Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The handwashing sheets ended the spread of colds at the school.
Most parents at Sunnyvale found the sheet helpful and read it.
Cold-related visits fell in the winter after the sheets went out.
The handwashing sheets caused the drop in visits for colds.
B.why: The text states that visits for colds fell 15 percent the winter the sheets were sent. That is directly supported; claims about cause or about most parents go further than the evidence.

whyNot.0: Overstatement: visits fell by 15 percent; colds did not stop spreading.
whyNot.1: Three phone calls cannot show what most parents thought.
whyNot.3: The passage shows the drop came after the sheets, not that the sheets caused it; other factors are not ruled out.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Carla Ruiz has volunteered at the county food bank every Saturday for six years. (2) She began by stacking cans in the warehouse. (3) Two years ago she started training new volunteers. (4) Last spring the director asked her to design the food bank's new delivery routes. (5) Carla says she still enjoys the quiet of the warehouse most.

Which sentence best supports the conclusion that the food bank's leaders have come to trust Carla with greater responsibility?
options: Sentence 4
Sentence 1
Sentence 5
Sentence 2
B.why: Being asked by the director to design the delivery routes shows leaders handing her a major task, the most direct proof of growing trust.

whyNot.1: Sentence 1 shows her commitment over six years, not the leaders' trust.
whyNot.2: Sentence 5 describes her own preference, which supports a different claim.
whyNot.3: Sentence 2 shows where she started; on its own it shows no added responsibility.

C.q:
Read the passage.

The town of Elm Ridge offered free smoke alarm installation to every household in 2023. Firefighters installed alarms in about 1,200 homes, mostly in older neighborhoods. In 2024, the town had the same number of house fires as in 2022, but no one died in a house fire in 2024, compared with three deaths in 2022.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: The program reduced the number of house fires in older areas.
Fire deaths fell after the program, though fires did not decline.
Every household in Elm Ridge received a free alarm during 2023.
Older neighborhoods had more fires than newer ones in 2024.
C.why: The passage gives the same number of fires in both years but zero deaths in 2024 versus three in 2022. The conclusion matches both facts and claims no more.

whyNot.0: This contradicts the passage: the number of house fires stayed the same.
whyNot.2: The offer went to every household, but alarms were installed in about 1,200 homes; the text never says all accepted.
whyNot.3: The passage never compares fire counts by neighborhood.

C.q:
Read the passage.

Pharmacist Lena Kowalski noticed that many older customers returned with questions about new prescriptions. She began spending two minutes with each first-time prescription, explaining the dose and showing the label. Over the next three months, return visits with questions fell by half, and the line at her counter grew slightly longer at peak hours.

Which statement, if it appeared in the passage, would CONTRADICT a conclusion the passage supports?
options: Lena explained each first-time prescription in about two minutes.
Most of Lena's first-time prescriptions went to older customers.
The peak-hour line at Lena's counter stayed the same length.
Customers who returned with questions were often older adults.
C.why: The passage says the line grew slightly longer at peak hours. A statement that the line stayed the same would contradict that supported detail.

whyNot.0: This agrees with the passage, which says she spent two minutes with each new prescription.
whyNot.1: The passage does not give this breakdown, so the statement neither contradicts nor confirms it.
whyNot.3: This matches the opening observation about older customers returning with questions.

C.q:
Read the passage.

Three community gardens opened in Fairview last year. At the Oak Street garden, neighbors who had never met now share tools and recipes. At the Pine Avenue garden, retirees teach teenagers how to plant tomatoes. At the Lake Road garden, families organized a harvest supper that drew 80 people.

Which conclusion is best supported by the examples in the passage?
options: Fairview's gardens have brought residents together.
Fairview's gardens produce most of the town's food.
Fairview's retirees enjoy gardening more than others.
Fairview should open a garden in each neighborhood.
C.why: Each example shows people connecting: neighbors sharing, retirees teaching teenagers, families hosting a supper. The conclusion generalizes what all three have in common.

whyNot.1: Food production for the town is never measured or mentioned.
whyNot.2: Retirees appear in one example; the passage compares no groups' enjoyment.
whyNot.3: This is a recommendation the author never makes; the passage describes, it does not propose.

reteach.title: Think like a detective
reteach.question: A detective says, 'The butler did it.' The judge asks, 'Which clue proves that?' How is that like a TEAS evidence question?

blocks.body: A detective's conclusion must explain every clue; one clue that does not fit sinks the case. And when the judge asks for proof, a clue that merely puts the butler in the house is weak. The muddy boots that match the garden prints are strong. TEAS evidence questions work the same way: the best evidence is the clue that points straight at the conclusion, not the one that only places you at the scene (the topic).

blocks.text: A clue that shares words with the conclusion is not automatically proof. Ask: if this sentence were true, would the conclusion have to follow?

explain.body: A conclusion is a judgment you reach by combining details. It must agree with every relevant detail and contradict none. If one sentence in the passage clashes with it, it is wrong, however reasonable it sounds.

test.q:
Read the passage.

After a city added bike lanes on Main Street, bike counts there doubled in a year. Shop owners on the street reported steady sales, and the number of crashes involving cyclists stayed about the same.

Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Cycling on Main Street grew without hurting local shop sales.
The bike lanes made Main Street much safer for every cyclist.
Shop owners on Main Street opposed the lanes before they opened.
Most residents of the city now ride bikes to work on Main Street.
test.why: Bike counts doubled and sales held steady: the conclusion combines both details and contradicts none.

whyNot.1: Crashes stayed about the same, so 'much safer' is not supported.
whyNot.2: The passage gives no information on what shop owners thought beforehand.
whyNot.3: Doubled bike counts on one street say nothing about most residents' commutes.

explain.body: The best evidence is the sentence that proves the exact claim most directly. Many sentences mention the topic; only one or two prove the point. Test each by asking: if this were true, would the claim follow?

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Our town's new walking trail opened in May. (2) It follows the old rail line for three miles. (3) Volunteers planted 200 native shrubs along the route. (4) A counter at the trailhead recorded 9,000 visits in the first summer. (5) Benches were added every half mile.

Which sentence best supports the conclusion that residents quickly embraced the trail?
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 5
test.why: Nine thousand visits in the first summer directly shows residents using the trail soon after it opened.

whyNot.0: Sentence 1 gives the opening date but no sign of use.
whyNot.1: Sentence 3 shows volunteer effort, which supports a different claim.
whyNot.3: Sentence 5 describes a feature of the trail, not how residents responded.

explain.body: Many options could be true in real life. The right answer is the one the text supports most strongly. Options that need outside knowledge, or that claim more than the text shows (all, proves, caused), are usually traps.

test.q:
Read the passage.

A dental office began texting reminders two days before appointments. That year, missed appointments fell from about 12 percent to 7 percent. The office also hired a second receptionist in the same year.

Which conclusion is most strongly supported?
options: The text reminders caused the drop in missed appointments.
Missed appointments fell in the year the reminders began.
The new receptionist reduced missed appointments by half.
Patients prefer text reminders to phone calls from staff.
test.why: The text directly shows missed appointments fell in the same year reminders started. Because a receptionist was also hired, it cannot show which change caused the drop.

whyNot.0: Two changes happened that year, so the text cannot pin the cause on the reminders.
whyNot.2: Nothing credits the receptionist, and 12 to 7 percent is not a drop by half.

explain.body: TEAS sets often ask for a conclusion, then for the sentence that best supports it. Answer Part 1 using the whole passage, then choose evidence that proves THAT conclusion, not a neighboring one.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Kevin started a study group for his anatomy class in September. (2) At first only three classmates came. (3) By November, twelve students attended each week. (4) The group's average quiz score rose from 71 to 83 over the term. (5) The instructor now mentions the group in every lecture.

A student concludes that the study group's members improved their quiz performance. Which sentence best supports that conclusion?
options: Sentence 3
Sentence 5
Sentence 2
Sentence 4
test.why: Sentence 4 reports the group's average quiz score rising from 71 to 83, the direct proof of improved quiz performance.

whyNot.0: Sentence 3 shows the group grew, which supports a claim about popularity.
whyNot.1: Sentence 5 shows the instructor's attention, not members' scores.
whyNot.2: Sentence 2 describes the small start and says nothing about performance.
